messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aisha was a 25-year-old South Asian woman who had been working as a counselor in the city when she first described the event that had changed the shape of her days. During a late-night bus ride home, after she had stayed on longer than usual because the streets were quiet and she did not want to walk alone, police officers boarded and began questioning passengers. What had started as an ordinary commute became, in her telling, a humiliating and frightening encounter in which she was singled out, handled roughly, and left feeling trapped in front of strangers. The bus itself, the hard smell of dust and earth drifting in from the open doors at a stop, and the sight of police uniforms became bound together in her mind with that night, so that later even the thought of riding the bus could bring back the scene with unnerving force. She said that when the memory returned, it did not come as a story she could place in the past; sometimes she could recall it and feel nothing at all, as if it had happened to someone else, and at other times it came back with all its sensations at once — the jolt in her chest, the sting of fear, the pressure of her body in the same position it had been in when she was cornered. Those moments left her convinced that people were not what they seemed, and that what had happened marked her as dirty or contaminated in some way she could not shake off, as though the encounter had taken something from her connection to her community and culture.

In the months that followed, Aisha began arranging her life around those reminders. If she saw a bus coming, noticed the smell of soil after rain, or spotted police near her route, she would change course, call a ride, or simply not go. She stopped meeting old friends from before the incident, because seeing people she had socialised with in that earlier life seemed to place her back near the person she had been before everything was altered. She covered her face with her hands when she felt exposed, and she kept checking mirrors in shop windows and car doors as if to reassure herself that no one was coming up behind her. Even her workday became narrower; as a counselor she could sit with other people’s distress, yet the commute to and from the office carried the possibility of a bus, a police car, or the smell of damp ground after a storm, and she found herself calculating routes with increasing care.

Aisha noticed that the more she tried to keep herself safe, the more her world seemed to confirm what she feared. Avoiding familiar friends and public spaces made her feel cut off from her community and culture, and that sense of loss fed the belief that the event had permanently separated her from other people. When she hid her face or scanned mirrors, she felt briefly less visible, but the very act of checking seemed to tell her that danger was always nearby and that she could not trust the ordinary faces around her. That suspicion deepened her sense that others were not what they seemed, and it made police presence on the street or in her neighborhood feel even more charged, as if any uniform could mean another loss of control. She had come to believe that her body now reacted to danger before her mind could catch up: her heart would kick up, her muscles would tighten, and only afterward would she realize that a bus had hissed to a stop or that an officer had walked past the window. At night she lay awake with the feeling that she needed to stay alert, because sleep felt like giving up her guard. In those sleepless hours the memory would surface again, and with it the same bodily position, the same shame, the same certainty that she was contaminated and that no one could be fully trusted. The flash of memory would sharpen her vigilance, and her vigilance would pull the memory back into focus, until even an outdoor smell drifting through an open window or the sight of a bus in daylight could be enough to send her into hiding again.

By the time she sought help, Aisha was exhausted by the tightening circle of bus routes avoided, friends left unanswered, mirrors checked, and nights spent listening for danger. She said she had come because she no longer wanted her life to be organized by police uniforms, public transport, and the conviction that she was somehow marked by what happened. What frightened her most was that this felt permanent; what she hoped for, though cautiously, was to be able to ride a bus, see familiar faces, and sleep without feeling she had to keep watch every second.
